1.g4.name: Grob's Attack
1.g4.background: Named after the Swiss master Henri Grob (1904–1974), who analysed it extensively and played hundreds of correspondence games with it; Carl Ahlhausen of Berlin was one of the first to play it, in the 19th century. Michael Basman beat John Nunn with it in 1978. Engines give Black a clear advantage after 1.g4.

1.g4 d5.strategy: Takes central space and eyes the g4-pawn with the c8-bishop at once. It is the sound reply: Black makes use of White's loosened kingside and forces White to say what the pawn is worth.

1.g4 e5.strategy: The instinctive centre grab, and a good one: Black builds a pawn centre of his own and can aim at the h4 square, which the g-pawn has left weak. It puts less direct pressure on White than hitting g4 does.

1.g4 g5.name: Grob's Attack: Double Grob
1.g4 g5.strategy: Copies White's move, so neither side has the better-placed kingside pawns. It is safe and keeps the balance, but Black gives up the chance to take the centre and to punish the loosened kingside.

1.g4 f5.name: Grob's Attack: Alessi Gambit
1.g4 f5.strategy: Attacks the g4-pawn at once, but White simply takes it. Black is a pawn down with a loosened kingside and not a single piece developed, so there is little to show for the gambit.

1.g4 d5 2.Bg2.name: Grob's Attack: Grob Gambit
1.g4 d5 2.Bg2.strategy: Gives the g4-pawn up for activity: the bishop takes the long diagonal and aims at d5 and, behind it, b7. White plays for quick pressure along that diagonal instead of defending the pawn.

1.g4 d5 2.h3.strategy: Protects the g4-pawn with a pawn instead of giving it up. White keeps the space gained on the kingside and a flexible set-up, but spends a tempo and leaves the g3 square weak.

1.g4 d5 2.e4.strategy: Offers a second pawn without any return. Black simply takes it, and the g4-pawn is still attacked by the c8-bishop, so White has two pawns to win back and nothing developed.

1.g4 d5 2.Bg2 c6.name: Grob's Attack: Grob Gambit Declined
1.g4 d5 2.Bg2 c6.strategy: Declines the pawn and shuts the bishop out: the c6-pawn guards d5 and blocks the long diagonal. Black keeps a solid pawn centre and makes White prove that g4 was worth a pawn.

1.g4 d5 2.Bg2 Bxg4.strategy: Takes the pawn with a developing move and accepts the gambit. The price is time and the b7-pawn: only the d5-pawn shields it from the bishop on g2, and White's compensation comes from that.

1.g4 d5 2.Bg2 h5.strategy: Challenges the g-pawn with the rook's pawn instead of the bishop. If White takes, Black recaptures with the rook, which then guards d5, but a move has gone into the flank and nothing is developed.

1.g4 d5 2.Bg2 e5.strategy: Takes the centre and leaves the g4-pawn alone for now. It is sound but slow, and it invites White to open the centre for the bishop while the g-pawn is still loose.

1.g4 d5 2.Bg2 Bxg4 3.c4.name: Grob's Attack: Grob Gambit, Fritz Gambit
1.g4 d5 2.Bg2 Bxg4 3.c4.strategy: Attacks d5 with a pawn: it is attacked by the pawn and the bishop and guarded only by the queen. If the pawn goes, the bishop takes aim at b7 and the rook behind it. White gives a second pawn for pressure on the long diagonal.

1.g4 d5 2.Bg2 Bxg4 3.c3.strategy: Prepares a solid pawn centre and quiet development instead of trying to win the pawn back at once. The compensation is slow: White gets a sound set-up but has no pressure on Black yet and a damaged kingside to look after.

1.g4 d5 2.Bg2 Bxg4 3.h3.strategy: Attacks the bishop and wins a tempo: ...Bxh3 loses the bishop to Bxh3, so Black has to retreat. White gains a little space, but Black keeps the extra pawn and loses nothing by stepping back, while the h-pawn does nothing for development.

1.g4 d5 2.Bg2 Bxg4 3.c4 d4.name: Grob's Attack: Romford Countergambit
1.g4 d5 2.Bg2 Bxg4 3.c4 d4.strategy: Black does not defend the d5-pawn but lets it step forward, which opens the bishop's way to b7 and the rook behind it. The idea is to give up the exchange and win time against the white kingside.

1.g4 d5 2.Bg2 Bxg4 3.c4 c6.strategy: The solid answer: the pawn gives d5 a second defender, so cxd5 meets a firm recapture and Black keeps the extra pawn without giving anything back. White has to show what the sacrifice buys, and the pressure on d5 and the long diagonal is all it has.

1.g4 d5 2.Bg2 Bxg4 3.c4 Nf6.strategy: Develops the knight and adds a second defender to d5, so cxd5 can be recaptured with the knight. But a knight on d5 becomes a target for White's queen and bishop, and Black has to defend with care against the pressure on d5 and b7.

1.g4 d5 2.Bg2 Bxg4 3.c4 d4 4.Bxb7.strategy: Takes the pawn the c8-bishop used to guard and attacks the rook on a8. White wins material at once but accepts a sharp fight: Black will give the exchange for the long diagonal and activity against a kingside with few pieces developed.

1.g4 d5 2.Bg2 Bxg4 3.c4 d4 4.Qb3.strategy: Doubles on b7 with the bishop: the pawn has no defender since the c8-bishop left for g4. Black has to spend time on it while White's queen and bishop work together, and the pressure on b7 and the long diagonal is the compensation for the pawn.

1.g4 d5 2.Bg2 Bxg4 3.c4 d4 4.Nf3.strategy: Develops and offers to trade Black's active bishop: after ...Bxf3 the bishop recaptures and bears on b7 again. White is still a pawn down with a damaged kingside, and Black keeps the extra pawn and the cramping d4-pawn.

1.g4 d5 2.Bg2 Bxg4 3.c4 d4 4.Bxb7 Nd7.strategy: Ignores the attacked rook and clears the knight off the back rank, so the queen can recapture on a8. Black gives the exchange on purpose and develops a piece at the same time.

1.g4 d5 2.Bg2 Bxg4 3.c4 d4 4.Bxb7 Na6.strategy: Clears b8 for the queen, but the knight lands on a6, where the b7-bishop attacks it and nothing guards it, since the a7-pawn blocks the rook. Bxa6 wins a whole piece, far more than the exchange Black meant to give.

1.g4 d5 2.Bg2 Bxg4 3.c4 d4 4.Bxb7 Bc8.strategy: Attacks the bishop, but the bishop on c8 and the knight on b8 both block the queen's way to a8. Bxa8 wins the whole rook, and Black has nothing to recapture with.

1.g4 d5 2.Bg2 Bxg4 3.c4 d4 4.Bxb7 Nd7 5..strategy: Takes the rook and wins the exchange. The cost is the king's bishop, which leaves the kingside and the long diagonal for good, and the recapture opens that diagonal for Black.

Pins the knight against the king and still attacks the rook, but Black moves the rook away and the bishop ends up trading itself for the pinned knight. White passes up the exchange for a level position.

Declines the rook to trade off Black's most active piece, the bishop on g4. White keeps the pawn it won, so material is level, and Black's rook comes to the half-open b-file. The exchange that was there for the taking is given up.

1.g4 d5 2.Bg2 Bxg4 3.c4 d4 4.Bxb7 Nd7 5..name: Grob's Attack: Grob Gambit, Fritz Gambit, Romford Countergambit
1.g4 d5 2.Bg2 Bxg4 3.c4 d4 4.Bxb7 Nd7 5..strategy: The queen recaptures straight onto the long diagonal and attacks the rook on h1, as the g2-bishop is gone. Black has given the exchange but gets the initiative against the undeveloped white kingside.
Attacks the bishop a second time instead of recapturing, but the bishop simply steps back to g2 and White is a whole rook up. Taking on a8 at once was the only way to avoid that.
Takes a pawn and attacks the queen, but Nxe2 or Qxe2 wins the bishop for it, and the queen still recaptures on a8 afterwards. Black loses a piece for a pawn on top of the exchange.

1.g4 d5 2.Bg2 c6 3.c4.strategy: Strikes at d5 again, now against a pawn that c6 guards. White wants the centre opened for the long diagonal, but the bishop is blocked for the moment and Black can simply take the pawn.

1.g4 d5 2.Bg2 c6 3.g5.name: Grob's Attack: Spike Attack
1.g4 d5 2.Bg2 c6 3.g5.strategy: Moves the pawn out of reach of the c8-bishop and takes kingside space, denying Black's knight the f6 square. The pawn is far advanced and hard to support, and nothing is developed.

1.g4 d5 2.Bg2 c6 3.h3.strategy: Defends the g4-pawn with the h-pawn, so ...Bxg4 now loses a piece to hxg4. White keeps the pawn and the bishop's diagonal and accepts a stretched kingside, which is the slow, solid way to continue the Grob: space on the wing and no material given away.

1.g4 d5 2.Bg2 c6 3.c4 dxc4.strategy: Takes the pawn and wins material, since the c6-pawn already blocks the long diagonal. White gets open lines for the pieces, but the extra pawn is real and Black has little to fear.

1.g4 d5 2.Bg2 c6 3.c4 Bxg4.strategy: Takes the gambit pawn at once and develops with it, while d5 and c6 keep the long diagonal shut for the moment. White's pressure on d5 and b7 only returns if the c-pawn trades on d5, so Black has to meet that break with care, but the extra pawn and the sound structure favour Black.

1.g4 d5 2.Bg2 c6 3.c4 Nf6.strategy: Develops the knight and adds a defender to d5, but g5 then attacks it and saves the g-pawn with a tempo. Black gives up the chance to win a pawn at once, and White's c-pawn keeps pressing on d5.

1.g4 d5 2.Bg2 c6 3.c4 dxc4 4.b3.name: Grob's Attack: Grob Gambit, Richter-Grob Gambit
1.g4 d5 2.Bg2 c6 3.c4 dxc4 4.b3.strategy: Attacks the c4-pawn to win the pawn back and opens the queen's bishop. But c6 shuts the g2-bishop out, so White is a pawn down for little in return, and Black can still take on b3.

1.g4 d5 2.Bg2 c6 3.c4 dxc4 4.Qa4.strategy: Hits the c4-pawn at once and puts pressure on c6 along the diagonal, keeping the queen in the fight for the pawn. Black can hold c4 with ...b5, which drives the queen back and loosens the queenside, so White's compensation is open lines for the pieces.

1.g4 d5 2.Bg2 c6 3.c4 dxc4 4.Qc2.strategy: Attacks the pawn from c2 and develops the queen, but ...b5 holds it and White has nothing to show for the pawn: the c6 pawn keeps the g2-bishop shut out.

1.g4 d5 2.Bg2 e5 3.c4.name: Grob's Attack: Spike, Hurst Attack
1.g4 d5 2.Bg2 e5 3.c4.strategy: Goes straight for d5, which is attacked by the pawn and the bishop and guarded only by the queen. It is the natural Grob plan of tearing at the centre for the long diagonal, at the price of a loose g-pawn.

1.g4 d5 2.Bg2 e5 3.d4.strategy: Strikes at the e5-pawn at once to open the centre for the bishop. But the g4-pawn is still hanging to the c8-bishop, and White has no lead in development to pay for it.

1.g4 d5 2.Bg2 e5 3.h3.strategy: Defends the g4-pawn with the h-pawn, so ...Bxg4 now loses a piece to hxg4. White keeps the pawn and accepts a stretched kingside, but nothing here challenges d5 or the centre, so Black can settle comfortably and block the bishop's diagonal.

1.g4 d5 2.Bg2 e5 3.d4 exd4.strategy: Takes the pawn and removes White's strike at the centre. Black keeps the extra pawn and a cramping pawn on d4, and the g4-pawn is still loose, so White has to find compensation quickly.

1.g4 d5 2.Bg2 e5 3.d4 e4.strategy: Blocks the long diagonal with a pawn that d5 supports, so the g2-bishop is shut in. Black gives up the pawn grab for space; the g4-pawn is still loose, and White must attack the chain from the side to free the bishop.

1.g4 d5 2.Bg2 e5 3.d4 Nc6.strategy: Develops with an attack on d4 and a second defender for e5, keeping the tension. It is sound and the loose g4-pawn is still there to take, but exd4 wins a pawn at once without letting White trade on e5.

1.g4 d5 2.Bg2 e5 3.d4 exd4 4.c3.name: Grob's Attack: Grob Gambit, Keres Gambit
1.g4 d5 2.Bg2 e5 3.d4 exd4 4.c3.strategy: Offers a second pawn to open lines and recapture with a developing move. It is a lot to give: if Black stays calm, White has little to show for two pawns.

1.g4 d5 2.Bg2 e5 3.d4 exd4 4.Qxd4.strategy: Recaptures at once with the queen, which now attacks d5 twice together with the bishop against one defender. White regains the pawn it gave and keeps the long diagonal open, so Black has to look after d5 before anything else.

1.g4 d5 2.Bg2 e5 3.d4 exd4 4.Nf3.strategy: Develops with an attack on d4 and keeps the queen at home, but Black can defend d4 with a developing move or take on g4 first. White is still a pawn down with a loose g-pawn and no clear compensation.

1.g4 d5 2.Bg2 h5 3.gxh5.name: Grob's Attack: Grob Gambit, Basman Gambit
1.g4 d5 2.Bg2 h5 3.gxh5.strategy: Takes the pawn, the natural answer, and it costs nothing new. Black recaptures with the rook, which also guards d5, so the pawn is soon returned and White is left with a damaged kingside structure.

1.g4 d5 2.Bg2 h5 3.g5.strategy: Pushes the attacked pawn out of reach of the h5-pawn and takes space, so Black's knight loses the f6 square. The pawn is far advanced and hard to support, and White has not developed a piece.

1.g4 d5 2.Bg2 h5 3.h3.strategy: Supports the g-pawn the way White does in other lines, but here White cannot hold it: after ...hxg4 hxg4 the h-file opens, Black trades rooks and wins the g-pawn with ...Bxg4, leaving White a clean pawn down.

1.g4 d5 2.h3 e5.strategy: Takes the centre and builds a broad pawn centre, rather than chasing the now guarded g4-pawn. Black can later close the long diagonal and make the white bishop's work hard.

1.g4 d5 2.h3 Nf6.strategy: Develops a piece and eyes the g4-pawn, which h3 now guards. White can answer by pushing the pawn on, gaining space with tempo, so Black loses time rerouting the knight; the move is sound but hands the Grob an easy gain of space.

1.g4 d5 2.h3 Nc6.strategy: A sound developing move that leaves the e-pawn free and asks White to show a plan. It blocks the c-pawn and puts off the central pawn that makes the long diagonal harmless, so Black is comfortable but not yet at the most accurate set-up.

1.g4 d5 2.h3 e5 3.Bg2.strategy: The standard set-up: the bishop takes its long diagonal with the g4-pawn safe behind h3. White intends to clear the centre of pawns so that the bishop can work.

1.g4 d5 2.h3 e5 3.c4.strategy: Strikes at d5 at once, in the spirit of the opening: tear at the centre so that the long diagonal opens. Black may take the pawn or push on and gain space, so White trades some structure for activity and must watch the loosened kingside.

1.g4 d5 2.h3 e5 3.d3.strategy: Opens the c1-bishop and prepares e4, but leaves Black's centre alone. With the kingside already loosened by g4 and h3, this slow set-up gives Black time to take space and aim at the weak squares.

1.g4 d5 2.h3 e5 3.Bg2 c6.name: Grob's Attack: Keene Defence
1.g4 d5 2.h3 e5 3.Bg2 c6.strategy: Supports d5 with a pawn so that Black can later close the long diagonal for good with a pawn on e4. A strong and solid reply, which takes the sting out of White's fianchetto.

1.g4 d5 2.h3 e5 3.Bg2 Nc6.strategy: The classical set-up: Black defends e5 with a developing move and lets White decide how to use the bishop. It avoids a pawn chain that White is likely to know well, at the price of leaving some pressure on d5.

1.g4 d5 2.h3 e5 3.Bg2 Nf6.strategy: Develops towards the centre and adds a guard to d5, but g5 kicks the knight at once. Black either retreats, losing time, or trades the knight for the bishop, which is acceptable but leaves White a cramping pawn on g5.

1.g4 d5 2.h3 e5 3.Bg2 c6 4.d4.strategy: Attacks the undefended e5-pawn and tears at the centre, the way the Grob is meant to work: if the centre is opened, the bishop gets its diagonal. It forces Black to decide what to do with the pawn.

1.g4 d5 2.h3 e5 3.Bg2 c6 4.c4.strategy: Attacks d5 from the side, in the Grob's way of undermining the centre so that the bishop gets its diagonal. If Black pushes the d-pawn the diagonal is blunted for good; if Black takes, White has to prove its compensation in activity.

1.g4 d5 2.h3 e5 3.Bg2 c6 4.d3.strategy: A modest preparation of e4 that keeps the position closed and solid. Without the central tearing that gives the Grob its point, the bishop stays blunted behind Black's pawns and Black is simply comfortable.

1.g4 d5 2.h3 e5 3.Bg2 c6 4.d4 e4.strategy: Answers the attack by shutting the long diagonal in the centre: the e4-pawn blocks the bishop and gains space. Black accepts a cramping pawn chain and a target for White to undermine.

1.g4 d5 2.h3 e5 3.Bg2 c6 4.d4 exd4.strategy: Opens the centre at once, which is what White's bishop wants. The queen recaptures in the middle and the pawn that could have closed the long diagonal is gone, so Black has traded a centre pawn for an easier game for White.

1.g4 d5 2.h3 e5 3.Bg2 c6 4.d4 Nd7.strategy: Defends e5, which the d4-pawn attacks and nothing guards yet, and develops, so that Black can retake on e5 with the knight. The d5 and c6 pawns stay intact, but White gets the open centre the bishop wants, and the knight on e5 has little to aim at.

1.g4 d5 2.h3 e5 3.Bg2 c6 4.d4 e4 5.c4.strategy: Strikes at the d5-pawn to undermine the chain that holds e4 and to open the bishop's diagonal again. It is the standard counter against a Black wall in the centre.

1.g4 d5 2.h3 e5 3.Bg2 c6 4.d4 e4 5.Nc3.strategy: Develops a piece and adds pressure on the e4 and d5 pawns, but it blocks the c-pawn and loses the usual strike at d5. The knight can also be pinned against the king by a bishop on b4.

1.g4 d5 2.h3 e5 3.Bg2 c6 4.d4 e4 5.Nd2.strategy: Develops while keeping the c-pawn free to strike at d5, and adds a piece to the pressure on e4. The price is a blocked c1-bishop, and White still has to find a way to undermine the chain.

1.g4 d5 2.h3 e5 3.Bg2 c6 4.d4 e4 5.c4 Bd.strategy: Develops the bishop on a diagonal that points at the dark squares the g-pawn left weak on White's kingside. Black gets a piece into play while keeping the centre closed.

1.g4 d5 2.h3 e5 3.Bg2 c6 4.d4 e4 5.c4 Nf.strategy: Adds a guard to both e4 and d5, the two pawns the chain rests on. But g5 chases the knight away at once, and the retreat costs time while White gains space on the kingside.

1.g4 d5 2.h3 e5 3.Bg2 c6 4.d4 e4 5.c4 f5.strategy: Props up e4 with a pawn, so the chain no longer depends on d5 alone. The price is a loosened kingside: the pawn can no longer guard e6 and g6, and White may open the g-file by taking on f5.

1.g4 d5 2.h3 e5 3.Bg2 c6 4.d4 e4 5.c4 Bd.strategy: Adds a second attacker to e4, which d5 alone guards, and to d5 itself. White increases the pressure on the chain from both ends and develops a piece.

Resolves the tension in the centre at once and gives up the pawn that was undermining the chain. Black recaptures with the c-pawn and gets a healthy centre and an open c-file, so White has traded away its main source of pressure for nothing concrete.

Adds a second attacker to e4 and keeps the c-pawn's pressure on d5, but the c1-bishop is blocked. Black can take on c4 and, because e4 then loses a guard, White gets the pawn back on the spot, with a level game.

1.g4 d5 2.h3 e5 3.Bg2 c6 4.d4 e4 5.c4 Bd.name: Grob's Attack: Keene Defence, Main Line
1.g4 d5 2.h3 e5 3.Bg2 c6 4.d4 e4 5.c4 Bd.strategy: Develops the knight to guard d5 and f5, so the chain holds against the pressure and the f-pawn is free to support e4. Black keeps the centre closed and plays for the kingside.
Defends e4 and d5 with a developing move, but g5 drives the knight back at once, and the retreat costs time. Black keeps the closed centre while White gains space on the kingside.
Props up e4 with a pawn, so the chain no longer relies on d5 alone. It commits a further pawn on the kingside, where White can trade it off by taking on f5, and the king's side is left looser.

1.g4 e5 2.Bg2.strategy: The natural follow-up: the bishop takes up its post on the long diagonal and fights for the centre from a distance, which is what the g-pawn's advance was meant to allow. White accepts a loosened kingside in return for pressure on the light squares.

1.g4 e5 2.h3.strategy: Supports the advanced pawn directly, so it cannot simply be attacked. The price is a second pawn move on the wing and slower development, while the weakened squares around White's kingside give Black targets for a knight and a free hand in the centre.

1.g4 e5 2.d3.strategy: Opens the c1-bishop onto Black's kingside and prepares e4, so that White fights for the centre with pawns as well as the bishop. It tries to do two things at once; with the g-pawn advanced White is still somewhat worse, but the position holds together.

1.g4 e5 2.c4.strategy: Claims space on the queenside and prepares a knight for c3 to hold d5. The advanced g-pawn is left to be defended, so Black has targets on the kingside.

1.g4 e5 2.Bg2 d5.strategy: Takes the centre with a second pawn and shuts the long diagonal, so the bishop on g2 meets a pawn on d5 and its pressure on the centre is blunted. Black holds the better share of the space and can develop at leisure, while White has to find a way to make something of the weakened kingside.

1.g4 e5 2.Bg2 h5.strategy: Attacks the g4-pawn at once and forces White to loosen the pawns on the wing. Taking on h5 opens the h-file for Black's rook, and pushing on to g5 loses the pawn to the queen.

1.g4 e5 2.Bg2 Nc6.strategy: A sound developing move that guards e5 and keeps the centre flexible. It does not challenge the fianchettoed bishop yet, but with the healthier pawn structure Black has little to fear while White finds a plan.

1.g4 e5 2.h3 Nc6.name: Grob's Attack: London Defence
1.g4 e5 2.h3 Nc6.strategy: A sound developing move that adds a defender to the e5 pawn and keeps the centre solid. It aims at no particular plan against White's kingside, but Black needs none: with the better pawn centre, simple development leaves White to prove the compensation.

1.g4 e5 2.h3 d5.strategy: Takes the centre with a second pawn and opens the bishop's diagonal, reaching the opening's main line by transposition. Black has the better pawn centre and the easier development, and White has to prove the compensation for the loosened wing.

1.g4 e5 2.h3 Ne7.strategy: Aims the knight at g6, from where it can reach f4 or h4, the squares the advanced pawns have left behind. Black disturbs White's kingside fianchetto before it is built and keeps the d-pawn flexible.

1.g4 g5 2.f4.name: Grob's Attack: Double Grob, Coca-Cola Gambit
1.g4 g5 2.f4.background: The origin of the name is uncertain; the first known online references to it are a German forum post and a chess.com forum post, both from 2008.
1.g4 g5 2.f4.strategy: Offers a pawn for nothing concrete: 2...gxf4 wins it, and White's own king is left exposed on the diagonal from e1 to h4 once Black opens the centre. White has no compensation for the lost pawn and the weakened kingside.

1.g4 g5 2.d4.strategy: Takes the centre and opens the c1-bishop onto the undefended g5-pawn, so Black has to look after it at once. White gets the initiative, though with the same pawn advance on both sides each king has a loosened wing.

1.g4 g5 2.Bg2.strategy: Takes the long diagonal and hits the b7-pawn, but Black's mirror-image reply puts a bishop on the same kind of diagonal against b2. Nothing has been gained, and the g5-pawn is left alone.
